name: Theory and construct development
proof: I developed the theory behind a COVID-19 field study, a study of fans and their favorite characters, a review of smartphones and wellbeing, my thesis, and my dissertation.

name: Experimental design
proof: I designed and ran six studies for my dissertation, with each plan registered in advance, and recruited more than 3,000 people. My master's thesis was a registered experiment with 305 participants.

name: Longitudinal and repeated-measures design
proof: I ran a 15-day behavior-change study with 560 people recruited and 455 retained. I also managed seven-day student diary studies, with about four surveys a day.

name: Causal and quasi-experimental methods
proof: I matched comparison groups on records for more than 100,000 students and used difference-in-differences terms in my longitudinal studies. Graduate courses trained me in regression discontinuity and instrumental variables.

name: Crossover trial analysis
also: Secondary analysis of a randomized trial
proof: I am first author on a 2026 paper analyzing a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of a ghrelin-receptor blocker in 29 people with alcohol use disorder. The NIH team designed the trial. I ran the analysis and made the figures.

name: Mixed-methods program evaluation
proof: I evaluated a university summer-skills program with focus groups, surveys, and student outcome data. I presented the results at departmental meetings.

name: Research synthesis
proof: I co-wrote a published review of how smartphones affect wellbeing. I synthesized the evidence for a COVID-19 social-contact paper and pooled the raw data from eight experiments.

name: Open and reproducible research
proof: I write my analysis plan down and register it publicly before I look at results. I share code and materials, and I co-founded a campus open-science group.

name: Digital behavior and technology effects
proof: I studied how phone use relates to face-to-face connection, wellbeing and sleep, and how time with close and distant contacts online related to stress during COVID-19.

name: Applied memory and cognition research
proof: In a graduate seminar, I turned theories of memory into a proposal for an applied study.

name: Socio-technical systems analysis
proof: In a graduate course, I traced how AI, cloud, and data systems depend on people and policy, through essays, a group project, and a final project.

name: Survey and questionnaire development
proof: I built the surveys for every study I have run and programmed them in Qualtrics. I wrote items for a published survey of why people play games.

name: Scale development and psychometrics
proof: I built the trust measures for my dissertation and a scale of how close people feel to their smartphones (in preparation, first author). I contributed to a published survey of gaming motivation and a VR symptom questionnaire.

name: Participant recruitment
proof: I recruit in person, through university pools, and on MTurk, CloudResearch and Prolific. I also handle recruitment administration for an NIH clinical trial.

name: Participant-centered communication
proof: I wrote the instructions and handled questions for general-public, student, online-panel and clinical-study participants.

name: Online-panel data quality
proof: I screen out inattentive and duplicate respondents. In a COVID-19 survey, 674 people consented and 569 completed it.

name: Behavioral intervention measurement
proof: I designed dissertation Study 6, which tracked trust, adherence, and behavior for 15 days. It showed no reliable difference between the doctor and AI conditions, and I reported it that way.

name: Content and media coding
proof: I coded video for prejudice in media, transcribed focus groups, and analyzed emotional speech in earlier lab roles.

name: Regression and multilevel modeling
proof: I fit linear, logistic, ordinal, negative-binomial, and mixed-effects models. In one analysis I pooled eight experiments (1,778 people) into a single multilevel model.

name: Core statistical tests
proof: I run t-tests, ANOVA, planned contrasts and chi-square tests, and I report effect sizes with them, in my thesis, my dissertation and my graduate statistics courses.

name: Mediation and moderation
proof: I tested who is affected and why. My dissertation used a multilevel mediated-moderation model, and my generative AI preprint used causal mediation.

name: Structural equation modeling
proof: I built latent-variable path models for an award-winning data competition entry, replicated a published model in R for a graduate course, and ran Mplus models for my dissertation.

name: Power and sensitivity analysis
proof: I plan sample sizes before each study and check what each one can detect. I taught a power-analysis workshop in 2023.

name: Robustness checks
proof: In my generative AI research, I tested the main result across 69 alternative analyses, so the conclusion does not rest on one analysis choice.

name: Blind outcome rating
proof: I designed blind ratings for my generative AI preprint. Judges who did not know the condition rated the work, and I compared quality with time spent.

name: Cross-study data integration
proof: I pooled eight experiments for a published analysis. Along the way I found and removed 173 placeholder rows.

name: Data cleaning and quality control
proof: I prepared the data for a study of fans and their favorite characters, for the pooled analysis, and for more than 100,000 student records.

name: Data visualization and dashboards
proof: I built Tableau dashboards that department chairs and administrators used each semester, and I made the figures for my generative AI preprint and this website.

name: Bayesian inference
proof: I use Bayes factors and Bayesian t-tests to show how strongly the data support a null result. They appear in my generative AI preprint and on the Studies 1 and 2 pages of this site.

name: Latent profile analysis
proof: I completed a 2023 workshop on latent profile analysis, a method that sorts people into groups by their pattern of answers.

name: Machine learning and prediction
proof: I built and tested classifiers in an end-to-end Python project for a graduate course, and I presented a poster on predicting app use.

name: Economic and cost-benefit analysis
proof: I applied cost-benefit and market-failure analysis to policy questions in two graduate economics courses.

name: R, Stata and SPSS
proof: R is my main language for modeling, figures and teaching. I used Stata across a graduate sequence in regression and program evaluation.

name: Cloud and API experiment engineering
proof: I host research tasks in the cloud and connect them to survey software. For one study, AWS linked Qualtrics to the ChatGPT API and stored each prompt and response.

name: Text analysis with dictionaries
proof: I ran LIWC text analysis at a university lab in 2018 and 2019. In my generative AI preprint, I compared human and AI writing with similarity scores.

name: Web, design and automation tools
proof: I wrote Excel macros and Praat scripts in earlier lab work. I build web pages, slides, and posters, including mrleitao.com and this site.

name: Modern text analysis
proof: I took a 2023 text-analytics workshop and a graduate course on word-frequency methods (TF-IDF) and language processing.

name: Python
proof: I used pandas, Jupyter, web scraping, and scikit-learn in a graduate data-science course. R is the language I use daily.

name: SQL
proof: I am building SQL skills through structured self-directed practice on DataLemur and Mode Analytics, and by translating my R code into SQL.

name: Geospatial analysis
proof: I mapped open Los Angeles County data in ArcGIS for a 2018 data competition entry.

name: Human-AI trust and reliance research
proof: My six-study dissertation compares trust in doctors and medical AI. It measures reliance by how far people move their own answer toward the advice.

name: Human-AI collaboration experiments
proof: I am co-first author on a preprint with two experiments (1,299 people) on drafting with generative AI versus editing its output. Work quality was similar. How people experienced the work was not.

name: Obedience to computer authority
proof: My master's thesis (305 participants) tested whether people obey computer instructors as readily as human ones. People obeyed both about equally, and I reported the null result.

name: Health and risk communication research
proof: I study how people read genetic-risk information. On a virtual-patient project (200 participants), I collected, cleaned, and analyzed the data.

name: Research program management
proof: I managed six to seven projects at once at Georgetown with a student team, and I now support six NIH projects.

name: Study operations
proof: I run studies from ethics approval through launch, monitoring and data handoff, for my own projects and for NIH collaborators.

name: Supervising and mentoring
proof: I have supervised research assistants since 2017, on teams of up to 15. I guided an honors thesis and served as a graduate mentor for a national psychology society.

name: Research governance
proof: I wrote and managed ethics-board protocols at two universities and support regulated clinical-study administration at NIH.

name: Clinical-study administration
proof: I support participant recruitment for an NIH clinical trial that tests a drug.

name: Recruitment operations

name: Workflow and process improvement

name: Grants and budgets

name: Grant-proposal writing

name: Policy analysis and memos

name: Consultative analysis

name: Workshop design and facilitation

name: Collaborative authorship
